title: Psalm 111: Great Are the Works of the LORD
summary: In a short alphabetic hymn, the psalmist gives thanks among the upright for God's works: his wonders, his provision, his covenant faithfulness, the land he gave, and the redemption he sent. The psalm ends with the famous saying that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
story: Psalm 111 begins a pair of alphabetic psalms (111 and 112) that follow the three psalms of David at the start of Book V. After the king's enthronement in Psalm 110, these psalms turn from royal victory to the steady goodness of God and the kind of life that answers it. Psalm 111 praises what God has done in Israel's history, recalling the exodus, the wilderness, Sinai, and the gift of the land without naming them outright. It gives the returned exiles of Book V a compressed memory of who God has been for his people, and it ends with a doorway into the wisdom of Psalm 112.
historical:
The psalm has no author in its heading; it opens simply with “Hallelujah!” Its alphabetic form, its dependence on older texts, and its closeness to wisdom writing lead many scholars to date it after the exile, in the Persian period, when the Psalter was taking its final shape and wisdom teaching flourished. Others note that acrostic poems also appear earlier, and that the psalm's content fits any period of Israel's worship. It was likely sung by the assembly in the temple.

The psalm alludes to events rather than narrating them. The wonders God caused to be remembered (verse 4) likely point to the exodus and to festivals such as Passover that were designed to remember it. Food for those who fear him (verse 5) recalls the manna in the wilderness. The inheritance of the nations (verse 6) is the land of Canaan. The redemption sent to his people (verse 9) points back to the rescue from Egypt, the great act of redemption in Israel's memory. The phrase gracious and compassionate in verse 4 echoes the LORD's self-description to Moses in Exodus 34:6.
cultural:
Israel's faith was shaped by remembering. Festivals, stories told to children, and songs like this one kept God's past acts present, so that each generation could say he redeemed us. The phrase in verse 4 that God caused his wonders to be remembered can be read literally as he made a memorial for his wonders, which many interpreters connect with the festivals. The council of the upright and the assembly in verse 1 are the gathered worshipers, the circle of the faithful and the larger congregation.

The fear of the LORD in verse 10 does not mean terror. In Israel's wisdom tradition it describes reverent awe and trust that leads to obedience, the right posture of a creature before the Creator. The same saying, that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom or knowledge, appears in Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10 and Job 28:28. Beginning can mean both starting point and first principle: wisdom starts here, and this is its most important part.
literary: Psalm 111 is an acrostic. After the opening Hallelujah, its twenty-two short lines begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, one letter per half-verse. In the Hebrew, verses 1 to 8 each hold two letters, and verses 9 and 10 hold three each. The form is a way of saying that the whole subject has been covered, from A to Z, and it made the psalm easy to memorize. Psalm 112 has exactly the same structure, and the two share phrases: what Psalm 111 says of God (his righteousness endures forever, he is gracious and compassionate) Psalm 112 says of the person who fears him. The psalm moves from a vow of praise, through the works of God, to the conclusion about wisdom.

outline.t: Thanks in the assembly of the upright
Food, covenant, and the gift of the land
The fear of the LORD, the beginning of wisdom

doctrines.note: Twice the psalm says God keeps his covenant forever (verses 5 and 9). His works in history are not random kindnesses but the actions of a God who has bound himself to his people by promise.
The psalm ends by placing wisdom on a religious foundation. Real understanding begins with reverence for God and grows by following his precepts, not by cleverness alone.
The psalm names God's character through his works: righteous, gracious, compassionate, faithful, just, holy, and awesome. Israel learned who God is by remembering what he had done.

words.note: Ma'aseh, work or deed. The word appears three times as the psalm's main subject: the works of the LORD are great, powerful, and true. It covers both creation and God's acts in history, and the psalm teaches that studying them, pondering them with delight, is itself an act of worship.

Berit, covenant, a binding relationship established by solemn promise. God remembers it (verse 5) and ordains it forever (verse 9). The covenant is the frame that gives God's deeds their meaning: he acts because he has committed himself.
Pedut, redemption, from a root meaning to ransom or buy back. It is used of the rescue from Egypt, where God freed his people from slavery. The word carries the idea of release secured at a cost.

Yir'ah, fear. In wisdom writing it describes reverent awe that shapes a whole life. It is joined here to obedience (following his precepts) and understanding, so fear of the LORD is not anxiety but the foundation of a well-ordered mind.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 111 directly, so the connections are thematic. The psalm praises God for sending redemption to his people and for keeping his covenant forever; the New Testament proclaims that in Jesus God has sent redemption in its fullest form and made a new covenant in his blood (Luke 1:68; 22:20). The food God gives to those who fear him recalls the manna, which Jesus himself takes up when he calls himself the bread of life (John 6). And Paul says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), so that the fear of the LORD that begins wisdom finds its center in knowing him.
questions: The psalm invites us to ponder God's works with delight. What works of God, in Scripture or in your own life, do you most need to remember right now?
What is the difference between fearing God and being afraid of him, and how does the first lead to wisdom?
The psalm is built to be memorized. What might change if you learned a psalm like this by heart?
